case_name: Moulton v. British Columbia (Ministry of Forests)
text:
IN THE SUPREME
COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

Moulton v. British Columbia (Ministry
of Forests),

2009 BCSC 1466

Date: 20091029

Docket:
S067611

Registry: Vancouver

Between:

Moulton Contracting Ltd.

Plaintiff

And

Her
Majesty the Queen in Right of the Province of British Columbia,

Sally Behn, Susan Behn, Richard Behn, Greg Behn, Rupert Behn, Lovey Behn, Mary
Behn, George Behn, Chief Liz Logan, on behalf of herself and all other members
of the Fort Nelson First Nation and the said Fort Nelson First Nation

Defendants

Before: The Honourable Mr. Justice Slade

Reasons for Judgment

In Chambers

Counsel for the Plaintiff:

K. Grist

Counsel for the Behn Defendants:

K.M. Brooks

Counsel for the Fort Nelson First Nation:

A. Rana

Counsel for the Province of British
Columbia:

J. Oliphant

Place and Date of Hearing:

Vancouver, B.C.

July 20, 2009

Place and Date of Judgment:

Vancouver, B.C.

October 29, 2009

INTRODUCTION

[
1
]

The Ministry of Forests for the Province issued
licences to Moulton that permitted a limited harvest of trees within defined sites
in the vicinity of Fort Nelson.

[
2
]

The sites to be logged are located in an area in
which members of the Fort Nelson First Nation (FNFN) exercise their hunting
rights, reserved to them by Treaty 8.

[
3
]

Ministry officials had consulted with the First
Nation during an earlier phase of the forest plan for logging in the area.  The
First Nation was not satisfied with the level of consultation, and wished to be
consulted further in relation to any proposed licence to harvest timber within
any site in the forest plan area.  It was not consulted in relation to the
licences issued to Moulton.

[
4
]

The Behn defendants are members of the FNFN.
They, or some of them, obstructed Moulton from entering the licence sites.

[
5
]

Moulton’s action against the Province claims
breach of contract and negligence.  Its claim against the Behns, and the FNFN,
is for unlawful interference with its exercise of the rights under the
licences, and conspiracy to harm its economic interests.

[
6
]

The Behn defendants, and the FNFN, say that the
licences, due to infringement of constitutionally protected treaty rights, are
invalid.

THE
APPLICATIONS

[
7
]

There are three applications for orders that
Moulton post security for costs.  Each of the Province, the Behn defendants,
and the FNFN, seek security in the approximate sum of $200,000, for a total
exceeding $600,000.

BACKGROUND

[
8
]

On June 27, 2006, the Province granted Timber
Sale Licence A66572, Timber Sale Licence A66573 and Road Permit No. R 15359 to
Moulton.  Moulton says that its entire work for the 2006 to 2007 winter season
relied on the TSLs.

[
9
]

Between September 19 and September 22, 2006,
Moulton mobilized its equipment to the TSL A66573 site, and commenced logging.

[
10
]

Between September 28, 2006, and October 1, 2006,
Moulton voluntarily stopped logging at the request of a representative of the
Ministry.

[
11
]

On October 2, 2006, some of the members of the
FNFN, including some members of the Behn family, prevented Moulton from
entering the area in which it had the right to log under the TSLs by blocking
the access road.

[
12
]

It is alleged that the actions of the FNFN
members, including the Behn family, prevented Moulton from cutting the timber
designated under the TSLs.  Moulton says that it lost all of the work it had
planned for the one year period from June 2006 until June 2007.  Moulton tried,
but was unable to find other work in Fort Nelson for the winter.

[
13
]

Moulton says that its inability to access the
areas designated for harvest caused it significant financial strain.  As a
result, the majority of Moulton’s equipment was sold at auction.  The proceeds
were used to pay the outstanding liabilities on the equipment.  Some of
Moulton’s equipment was repossessed.  Prior to the blockade, Moulton had not
missed any payments for its equipment, and no collections proceedings had previously
been brought against it for any of its equipment.

[
14
]

Moulton says that its inability to harvest
resulted in a $1,115,757 loss in the 2006-2007 fiscal year.  It now has no
assets, and lacks the means to borrow money or otherwise raise the funds
necessary to post security for costs.

[
15
]

Kevin Moulton is the sole officer, director and
shareholder of Moulton.  He says that he is not able to raise the funds
necessary to post the security for costs sought by the defendants.  If Moulton
is ordered to post security, it will be unable to pursue this action.

[
16
]

Between July 31, 2006, and October 3, 2006,
George Behn and other members of the FNFN had advised the Ministry of Forests
that they considered the consultation that had taken place over plans to permit
the harvesting were inadequate.  They did not want harvesting on the TSLs.

[
17
]

On examination for discovery, a representative
of the Ministry testified that consultation with the FNFN was done in relation
to an amendment to the Forest Development Plan.  The issuance of TSLs is made
pursuant to the Plan.  It is not the practice of the Ministry to consult
further on the advertising and sale of the individual TSLs.

[
18
]

On examination for discovery, George Behn said
that he spoke with the Chief and Council of the FNFN prior to blocking
Moulton’s access to the harvesting areas.  He informed the Chief and Council of
his intentions.  He testified that the Chief of the FNFN told him that this was
a good idea, as it would establish a basis for a test-case.

[
19
]

Documents produced on discovery include an
e-mail from Laurie Montour, the Director of the FNFN Land and Resources
Department, to the defendant Susan Behn, a member of the FNFN, in which it is
stated that George Behn is at the band office, and had been given the ‘go
ahead’ from Chief and Council to shut down logging on his trap line.  The
minutes of the October 2, 2006, meeting include the following:

George Behn joined
meeting concerned of logging on his trapline without his consent.  Darryl read
out letter received by Bill Warner, Northern Interior Forest Region regarding
cancelling timber sales.  George explained that there is some work being
continued on his land.  George Behn and Laurie, Director of Lands and Resources
are to visit the area of where the work is being done and to stop the logging.
Chief and Council are in support to stop the work being done on his land.
George explains that he wants studies done.  He has trails and some spiritual
rocks on his land.

[
20
]

At a meeting on November 15, 2006, between the
FNFN, the Behns, and Provincial Ministry officers, Chief Logan is said to have
stated:

You know our
stance.  Do you want to see more blockades?

[
21
]

George Behn, and Sally Behn, a member of the
Council of the FNFN, both acknowledged on discovery that they knew that by
setting up the blockade, Moulton would be prevented from logging, and would
suffer an economic loss.  Both acknowledged that they had no issue with
Moulton; their issue was with the Provincial Ministry that granted the TSLs.

[
22
]

The material on this application reveals that
George Behn, and the Chief and Council of the FNFN, were aware that the legal
remedies of injunction and judicial review could be pursued to prevent the
exercise of Moulton’s rights under the TSLs.

THE
CLAIMS, AND DEFENCES

[
23
]

Moulton claims against the Province for breach
of contract and negligence.  The negligence claim engages the question of the
duty and standard of care in circumstances in which a Crown ministry issues a
forest tenure when there is known to be a potential conflict with the exercise
by Aboriginal peoples of their treaty rights.

[
24
]

The essence of Moulton’s claim against the Behn
defendants and the FNFN is that they wilfully interfered with the exercise of
its rights under the TSLs and road permit, and caused them direct economic
loss.

[
25
]

The Province denies breach of contract and
negligence, and points to the actions of the Behn defendants as the cause
Moulton’s loss.  The Behn defendants and the FNFN say that Moulton’s losses are
the fault of the Province for its failure to adequately consult in relation to
the impact of timber harvesting on their exercise of hunting rights.

[
26
]

None of the defendants fault Moulton for its
predicament.

[
27
]

In defence to Moulton’s action, the Behn
defendants and the FNFN claim infringement of treaty rights, and challenge the
authority of the Province to issue the TSLs and road permit.  The Behns say
that the cumulative impact of the exercise of resource tenures granted by the
Province strikes at the core of their constitutionally protected treaty rights,
such that the legislation authorizing the grant of the TSLs and road permit are
constitutionally inapplicable to the extent that their provisions result in
further infringement of treaty rights.

[
28
]

The bills of costs presented by each defendant
are based on a 49 day trial.  Were it not for the reliance by the Behn
defendants and the FNFN on defences that raise treaty rights and infringement,
this would be a short trial.  Without a treaty rights based defence, it seems
at this stage that the Behn defendants would have no defence.  Their actions,
or the actions of some of them, and causation of the losses sustained by
Moulton, could be established in a day.

[
29
]

The case as against the FNFN alleges conspiracy
to harm the plaintiff’s economic interests.  The proof of conspiracy, and the
liability of the collective for the actions of a few are somewhat complex, but
are issues of law that do not take a great deal of evidence to frame.

[
30
]

As I understand Moulton’s action against the
Crown, its claim of breach of contract and negligence rests primarily on the
Province’s failure to consult with the FNFN in relation to the issuance of the
TSLs and road permit.  The evidentiary base to frame the legal issue will not
require a lengthy trial.  The Province acknowledges that it did not consult
with the FNFN in relation to the TSLs.  It relies on the adequacy of
consultation in relation to the Forest Development Plan.

[
31
]

In short, the Behns appear to have no arguable
defence except that based on infringement of treaty rights.  At present, the
evidence and pleadings, as they concern the FNFN, indicate an arguable defence
based on the application of the law to facts that are not seriously in issue.
The time consuming issue raised by the FNFN is infringement.

[
32
]

The presence of treaty right based defences take
this from a one week trial in which most of the evidence would be limited to
that relevant to the issues between Moulton and the Province, to a ten week
trial.  This will include evidence of those who have experienced a decline in
the traditionally harvested resources, and expert evidence.

THE LAW,
APPLIED

Sanderson
and
Bullock
Orders

[
33
]

Moulton submits that it would be entitled to a
Bullock

or
Sanderson
order in this action because it will be successful against
one or more of the defendants.  It says:

Moulton is an
innocent party that in no way contributed to or caused the blockade, and as a
result of one or more of the defendants’ conduct it has suffered loss.

[
34
]

I will assume, for the present purposes, that
the potential for the availability of such an order is a relevant consideration
on an application for security for costs.

[
35
]

Where there are multiple defendants, R. 57(18)
enables the court to order that the unsuccessful defendant(s) pay the costs of
the successful defendant:

(18)      Where
the costs of one defendant against a plaintiff ought to be paid by another
defendant, the court may order payment to be made by one defendant to the other
directly, or may order the plaintiff to pay the costs of the successful
defendant and allow the plaintiff to include those costs as a disbursement in
the costs payable to the plaintiff by the unsuccessful defendant.

[
36
]

These are generally referred to as
Sanderson

or
Bullock
orders (named after
Sanderson v. Blythe Theatre Co.
,

[1903] 2 K.B. 533 (C.A.)
and
Bulluck v. London General Omnibus Co.
,

[1907] 1 K.B. 264 (C.A.)
, respectively).  A
Sanderson
order requires an
unsuccessful defendant to pay the costs of any successful defendant, whereas a
Bullock

order allows the plaintiff to recover from the unsuccessful defendants those
costs that it is required to pay to the successful defendants.  The difference
in the orders lies in who bears the risk of an inability to collect, but the
end result is the same if collection is possible (see
Home Equity et al v.
Crow et al.
,
2005 BCSC 743
at paras.
75-78
, 14 C.P.C. (6th) 203).

[
37
]

The threshold test for establishing an
entitlement to a
Sanderson
or
Bullock
order has been
traditionally described as whether “it was reasonable for the plaintiff to have
joined the successful defendant in the action”:
Robertson v. North Island
College Technical and Vocational Institute
(1980),
1980 CanLII 2581 (BC CA)
, 119 D.L.R. (3d) 17
(B.C.C.A.) at 23 per Lambert J.A.  More recently the Court of Appeal has refined
this test to require a connection between the conduct of the unsuccessful
defendant and the reason for the successful defendant being brought into the
litigation.  The Court of Appeal, in
Grassi v. WIC Radio Ltd.
,
2001 BCCA
376
, 89 B.C.L.R. (3d) 198, held that this connection exists where the
unsuccessful defendant points the finger at the successful defendant.  (See
Times
Square Holdings Ltd. v. Shimizu
,
2001 BCCA 667
, 95 B.C.L.R. (3d) 234, and
Gill
v. Dunlop-Miller
,
2004 BCCA 632
, 33 B.C.L.R. (4th) 325, supplementary
reasons at
2005 BCCA 90
))

[
38
]

If a plaintiff can successfully establish this
factor, then the court has the discretion to determine what distribution of
costs would be just.

[
39
]

It is not, in my respectful opinion, possible to
determine at this stage of the proceeding that the plaintiff is certain of
success against one or more of the defendants.  The potential for a
Sanderson

or
Bullock
order does not obviate the need to consider an award of
security for costs.

Security
for Costs

[
40
]

The court is empowered to grant security for
costs against a plaintiff corporation by
s. 236
of the
Business Corporations
Act
, S.B.C. 2002, c. 57:

236      If a
corporation is the plaintiff in a legal proceeding brought before the court,
and if it appears that the corporation will be unable to pay the costs of the
defendant if the defendant is successful in the defence, the court may require
security to be given by the corporation for those costs, and may stay all legal
proceedings until the security is given.

[
41
]

In
Fat Mel’s Restaurant Ltd. v. Canadian
Northern Shield Insurance Co.
(1993),
1993 CanLII 1669 (BC CA)
, 76 B.C.L.R. (2d) 231, 25 B.C.A.C. 95,
Proudfoot J.A., for the court, said at para 16:

The making of
an order under s. 229 of the
Company Act
is discretionary.  However,
once the applicant for security has shown that the plaintiff will not be able
to pay costs should the claim fail, security is generally ordered unless the
court is satisfied that there is no arguable defence.  . . .

[
42
]

The decision to order security for costs is
discretionary.  In
Kropp v. Swaneset Bay Golf Course Ltd.
(1997),
1997 CanLII 4037 (BC CA)
, 29
B.C.L.R. (3d) 252 at para.
17
, 90 B.C.A.C. 170, the Court of Appeal adopted the
factors for consideration set out by the English Court of Appeal in
Keary
Development v. Tarmac Construction
,
[1995] 3 All E.R. 534 at 539-542
:

…

1.         The
court has a complete discretion whether to order security, and will act in
light of all the relevant circumstances;

2.         The
possibility or probability that the plaintiff company will be deterred from
pursuing its claim is not without more sufficient reason for not ordering
security;

3.         The
court must attempt to balance injustices arising from use of security as an
instrument of oppression to stifle a legitimate claim on the one hand, and use
of impecuniosity as a means of putting unfair pressure on a defendant on the
other;

4.         The
court may have regard to the merits of the action, but should avoid going into
detail on the merits unless success or failure appears obvious;

5.         The
court can order any amount of security up to the full amount claimed, as long
as the amount is more than nominal;

6.         Before
the court refuses to order security on the grounds that it would unfairly
stifle a valid claim, the court must be satisfied that, in all the
circumstances, it is probable that the claim would be stifled; and

7.         The lateness of the application
for security is a circumstance which can properly be taken into account.

[
43
]

In
Kropp
,
supra,
Finch J.A., for
the court, refered to the earlier decision in
Fat Mel’s, supra
, and
observed, at para. 11, that:

… The corporate
plaintiff’s lack of assets, the very foundation of a defendant’s application
for security, cannot be used to defeat its claim to security.  The law does not
treat corporate plaintiffs with the same generosity and flexibility as natural
persons opposing an application for security.

[
44
]

The genesis of the law of security for costs as
it applies to corporate plaintiffs is identified in para. 16 of
Kropp
.
There, Finch J.A. refered to the “leading English decision” of
Pearson v.
Naydler,
[1977] 3 All E.R. 531 (Ch. D.)
.  Vice-Chancellor Megarry referred
to some basic principles at pp. 533, 535:

The basic rule
that a natural person who sues will not be ordered to give security for costs,
however poor he is, is ancient and well-established.  As Bowen LJ said in
Cowell
v. Taylor

(1885), 31 Ch.D. 34 at 38,
both at law and in equity ‘the general
rule is that poverty is no bar to a litigant’.  The power to require security
for costs ought not to be used so as to bar even the poorest man from the
courts.  …

In the case of a
limited company, there is no basic rule conferring immunity from any liability
to give security for costs.  The basic rule is the opposite; s. 447 applies to
all limited companies, and subjects them all to the liability to give security
for costs.  The whole concept of the section is contrary to the rule developed by
the cases that poverty is not to be made a bar to bringing an action.  There is
nothing in the statutory language (the substance of which goes back at least as
far as the
Companies Act
1862 s. 69) to indicate that there are any
exceptions to what is laid down as a broad and general rule for all limited
companies.  Nor is it surprising that there should be such a rule.
A man
may bring into being as many limited companies as he wishes, with the privilege
of limited liability; and s. 447 provides some protection for the community
against litigious abuses by artificial persons manipulated by natural persons
.
One should be as slow to whittle away this protection as one should be to
whittle away a natural person’s right to litigate despite poverty.

[Emphasis added]

[
45
]

In the present matter, it could hardly be said
that Moulton’s claim falls within the category of litigious abuses by
artificial persons manipulated by natural persons that concerned the court in
Pearson
v. Naydler, supra
.

[
46
]

The assertion in
Fat Mel’s
that security
is generally ordered unless the court is satisfied that there is no arguable
defence is modified by the adoption by the Court of Appeal, in
Kropp
,
of
the factors from
Keary Development
,
supra.
This includes the
consideration of whether an order for security would unfairly stifle a valid
claim.

[
47
]

There is another consideration.  A link between
the defendant’s actions and the plaintiff’s impecuniosity has a bearing on the
exercise of discretion to decline to order security for costs: see
Grant v.
Henderson Development (Canada) Ltd.
,
2003 BCSC 1473
at para.
19
:
Scotford
Electrical et al v. Blue Mountain Log Sales et al.
,
2005 BCSC 538
at paras.

23-29
;
Gold River Chinook Project Society v. Bowater Pulp & Paper Canada
Inc.
,
2002 BCSC 166
at paras.
32 and 34
.

[
48
]

In
Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v.
Canadian Jewish Congress
(1999),
1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, 36 C.P.C. (4
th
) 266 (B.C.S.C.),
Romilly J., at para. 14, set out the following criteria for consideration in an
application under what is now s. 236 of the
Business Corporation Act
:

1.         Does it appear that the plaintiff company will be unable
to pay the  defendants’ costs if the action fails?

2.         If so, has the plaintiff shown that it has exigible
assets of sufficient value to satisfy an award for costs?

3.         Is the court satisfied that the defendants have an
arguable defence to present?

4.         Would an
order for costs visit undue hardship on the plaintiff such that it would
prevent the plaintiff’s case from being heard?

[
49
]

The first three factors are preconditions to the
court’s discretion to order security for costs, and the fourth factor arises
when the court considers exercising its discretion on the basis of the factors
in
Kropp
.  Romilly J. went on to explain what the court should consider
in deciding whether it should exercise its discretion (at para. 21):

In exercising
its discretion to order security for costs, the court must consider the
interests of justice between the parties and balance those interests to try to
insure that the substance of their dispute ends up properly litigated.  As
such, once a
prima facie
case is made out by the defendants, the court
must consider whether an undue hardship would be visited upon the plaintiff if
an award for security for costs was made.  In other words, would the ordering
of security for costs prevent justice from being done.

The
Citizens for Foreign Aid Criteria

[
50
]

The first two criteria are met, as:

1.         It appears that Moulton will be unable to pay the
defendants’ costs if the action fails; and

2.         Moulton has not shown that it has exigible assets of
sufficient value to satisfy an award of costs.

[
51
]

The following criteria then fall to be
considered:

1.         Do the defendants have an arguable defence to present?
and

2.         Will an order for costs visit undue hardship on Moulton
such that it would prevent its case from being heard?

The Behn
Defendants

[
52
]

The evidence on examination for discovery
establishes that George Behn, and others associated with him, acted in a way
that obstructed Moulton’s exercise of rights conferred by the TSLs and road
permit.  It was known that this would result in financial loss to the
plaintiff.

[
53
]

The only defence available to these defendants
must be based on infringement of treaty rights.  While a question may arise as
to whether proof of a potential for infringement is a defence to a claim for
damages, it cannot be said at this stage of the proceeding that there is no
arguable defence.

[
54
]

There is a natural sympathy with the present
circumstances of persons of Aboriginal descent who are sustained materially and
culturally by hunting rights recognized and reserved by treaty.  The
incremental accumulation of encroachments on the exercise of such rights has
been recognized as a significant infringement (
R. v. Gladstone
,
1996 CanLII 160 (SCC)
, [1996] 2
S.C.R. 723 at para.
52
.

[
55
]

However, Aboriginal peoples are part of a
community in which conflicting interests are reconciled, where discussion
fails, through the process of the law.  The FNFN and Mr. Behn, although
dissatisfied with the consultation in relation to the Forest Development Plan,
and despite their knowledge that the Ministry did not intend to consult
further,, did not seek judicial review of the decision of the Ministry to grant
the TSLs.  Since the decision in
Haida Nation v. British Columbia (Minister
of Forests),
2004 SCC 73
, [2004] 3 S.C.R. 511, judicial review has often
been employed to address concerns around infringement, consultation, and
accommodation.  The choice to take direct action to obstruct the exercise of
rights under a forest tenure in circumstances in which judicial review, which
would place the issue squarely between the First Nation and the Province, is,
in my opinion, a relevant consideration within the first factor in
Kropp
,

supra.

[
56
]

George Behn’s reliance on the communal rights
protected by Treaty 8 expands the scope of this litigation.  The Behn
defendants’ estimate of costs, $200,000, is driven almost entirely by their
reliance on a claim of infringement of treaty rights.

[
57
]

The actions of George Behn and others associated
with him have caused the impecuniosity of the plaintiff.  An order for costs
would prevent the plaintiff’s case from being heard.

[
58
]

The Behn defendants’ application for security
for costs is dismissed.

The Fort
Nelson First Nation (FNFN)

[
59
]

The evidence on examination for discovery, and
the documentary evidence, tends to establish the participation in the blockade
of the members of the First Nation, at the instance of the First Nation’s
governing body.

[
60
]

Legal questions arise on the issue of whether
the actions of individuals who are members of the collective, in these
circumstances, establishes the liability of the collective.  This issue is
raised by para. 10 of the FNFN statement of defence, in which it is stated, in
part, that:

The FNFN says
that it is not vicariously liability [sic] for the conduct of its members and
the FNFN has no legal power or duty to control the actions of its members.

[
61
]

While this may be an arguable defence, it arises
on a body of evidence that will consume very little time at trial.  The time
consuming defence, and the one that drives the FNFN’s $200,000 estimate of
costs, is the plea of infringement of treaty rights.

[
62
]

The FNFN, although aware of the legal avenues of
injunction and judicial review, did not avail themselves of either.

[
63
]

The evidence on examination for discovery and
disclosure of documents reveals the involvement of  the governing body of the
First Nation in the obstruction of the exercise of the plaintiff’s rights.
Hence, the FNFN is implicated in the plaintiff’s impecuniosity.

[
64
]

There is no question but that an award of
security for costs of the magnitude sought would stifle the plaintiff’s claim.

[
65
]

The application of the FNFN for security for
costs is dismissed.

The Crown
in Right of the Province of British Columbia

[
66
]

Moulton’s claim against the Province is for
breach of contract and negligence.

[
67
]

To succeed in negligence, Moulton must establish
that the Province owed a duty of care to the plaintiff to consult with the
FNFN, and failed to do so to a requisite standard.  A determination of the
standard of care may not be a simple matter.

[
68
]

I note, in this regard, that the Province did
consult with the FNFN regarding the Forest Development Plan, but not with
regard to the TSLs granted pursuant to that plan.

[
69
]

As for the claim for breach of contract, the
plaintiff asserts that it is an implied term of the contract that it consult
with the FNFN.

[
70
]

As it has not been determined that the Province
breached the contract or was negligent, a nexus between the acts or omissions
of the Province and Moulton’s impecuniosity has not been established.

[
71
]

The Province has an arguable defence.

[
72
]

In
Apex Mountain Resort Ltd. v. British
Columbia
,
[1998] B.C.J. No. 1918 (S.C.)
, Bauman J., as he then was,
said:

46        In
Keary
the court said
this (at 540):

However, the
court should consider not only whether the plaintiff company can provide
security out of its own resources to continue the litigation, but also whether
it can raise the amount needed from its directors, shareholders or other
backers or interested persons.  As this is likely to be peculiarly within the
knowledge of the plaintiff company, it is for the plaintiff to satisfy the
court that it would be prevented by an order for security from continuing the
litigation (see
Flender Werft AG v. Aegean Maritime Ltd.
,
[1990] 2
Lloyd’s Rep 27
